analysis.one_liner: Lets USDA fine meat and poultry plants up to $100,000 for food safety violations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the House and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the meat and poultry inspection laws, the Agriculture Secretary's main enforcement tools were limited — largely criminal prosecution or shutting off inspection, which shuts down a plant. This bill would have added a middle option: civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted separately. Fines could account for the seriousness of the violation, the firm's culpability, its size, and its history, and companies would get a hearing and court review before paying.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who eat meat and poultry. Faster, more flexible enforcement against plants with unsafe practices could reduce the risk of contaminated meat reaching grocery shelves, and repeated daily violations could add up for serial offenders.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to assess civil money penalties of up to $100,000 per violation of the Federal Meat Inspection Act or the Poultry Products Inspection Act, with each day a violation continues counted as a separate offense.
Requires the Secretary to weigh the gravity of the violation, the firm's culpability, the size and type of the business, and its history of prior offenses, so penalties can be scaled to the offender.
Lets the Secretary use fines instead of the existing all-or-nothing enforcement choices, and preserves the option of withdrawing inspection from a company that refuses to pay a final penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Meatpacking and poultry processing firms that violate inspection rules would face fines of up to $100,000 per violation, plus possible loss of federal inspection — which would stop their operations — if they do not pay. Taxpayers fund the enforcement apparatus either way.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows the Secretary to use civil penalties in place of referring violations for prosecution when the Secretary believes the public interest is adequately served, which critics could argue risks letting serious repeat violators buy their way out of criminal accountability.

Fines can be priced in as a cost of doing business by large processors; a $100,000 penalty is a small share of revenue for a major meatpacking firm, so the deterrent effect on the largest violators may be limited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, targeted food-safety upgrade: it gives regulators a proportionate tool short of shutting a plant down, with due process built in. The main legitimate concern is that fines alone may not deter the largest processors, and the option to substitute fines for prosecution could soften enforcement in the wrong hands. On balance the costs fall on violators and the benefits accrue to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its livestock subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nita Lowey introduced the bill in the House on August 5, 1999, joined by Rep. Thompson of Mississippi.
The House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture the same day, and a week later to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture.
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors avoided a new fine regime that could have reached $100,000 per violation, per day, and continued operating under the existing enforcement rules. Consumers did not get the added food-safety tool.

for.name: Rep. Nita Lowey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give USDA civil money penalty authority over meat and poultry inspection violations.

for.name: Rep. Bennie Thompson
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 5, 1999 and never brought the bill to a markup or vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 11, 1999 and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and the bill attracted only one cosponsor; no votes were ever recorded, so the partisan shape of opposition is unknown from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed violating plants to fines of up to $100,000 per violation, per day, and to withdrawal of inspection for nonpayment. Processors gained nothing from the bill's death, which left the weaker existing enforcement status quo in place.

Consumers and the retailers who sell them meat and poultry lose the prospect of stricter deterrence against contaminated product. The bill's failure leaves inspection enforcement without a graduated fine option.
